newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: SOCCER-DUKLA AIM FOR NEW GLORIES IN MODERN ERA.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DUKLA AIM FOR NEW GLORIES IN MODERN ERA.

text.p: Dukla Prague, once the pride of Czech soccer, became little more than another former East Bloc army team after the fall of Communism in 1989. But all that may be about to change.

European Cup semifinalists in 1967, Dukla Prague won the Czechoslovak first division championship 11 times and finished runners-up seven times after the club was established by the Ministry of Defence in 1948.
They even inspired a cult following abroad which shaped the quirky Half Man-Half Biscuit record "All I want for Christmas is a Dukla Prague away kit" in the 1980s.

But the fall of Communism in 1989 saw free-market realities replace Soviet-style sports funding and the army team, named after a mountain pass in former federation partner Slovakia where the Czechs and Slovaks battled Nazis to the death, went into freefall.
Out of the first division and way down the ladder to the lowly ranks of the amateur third division where they languished until local entrepreneur Bohumil Duricko recently took over the team.

"I hesitated whether to buy Dukla or a helicopter" is his standard jokey response to questions asking why he took over the troubled team. But he is genuinely excited about the future and he continues with energy.
"This club has sent more players to the national team than any other and had more international success," he said.
"We want to return the club to those traditions. To return to the first division would help create a new tradition."

At their peak, life was easy for Dukla. With the likes of Josef Masopust, European Footballer of the Year in 1962, and Zdenek Nehoda, a record 90 caps for his country, they would fill the major 25,000-seat venues.
And when they needed new players they could ignore the transfer market by simply drafting them into the army where they became the country's best-compensated athletes.
But despite their success, that attitude also made them the most reviled team in the country, a symbol of the militarist regime, and there were few tears as their fortunes faded.
By the end of the 1993-4 season, when they slipped to the third division and were forced to sell off players, the spectators were almost outnumbered by the stadium staff.
Duricko's first move to restore the club to former glories was to buy second division club FC Pribram. He merged the teams and then expropriated Pribram's spot in the higher league.
It may take time but he is confident about his chances of changing Dukla's image.
"Who liked the army then? Today, the club has nothing in common with the army and that's important," he said.

Dukla have returned to winning ways in the second division. With a group of young players, most of whom have little recollection of Dukla's chequered past, they have won 12 of their 17 games to lead the race for first division promotion.
"When Dukla left the league it was sad in a way. But now things have changed and it would be good to see them return," said Frantisek Cernoch, a local soccer historian.
Ultimately, it may even lead to a return to the top flight of European soccer and, who knows, another cult record.
